title: Before dawn, a hymn to Christ
author: Pliny the Younger

edition.name: Pliny, Selected Letters, Dickinson College Commentaries, "Edited by Ashley Roman Francese" (as credited on the page); the page does not name the critical edition its Latin follows. Macronized text; DCC content is published under a Creative Commons BY-SA licence, though the letter pages themselves carry no licence line
edition.section: Letter 10.96.7 (first sentence) and Trajan's reply 10.97.2 (first sentence)

source_text: Adfirmabant autem hanc fuisse summam vel culpae suae vel erroris, quod essent soliti stato die ante lucem convenire, carmenque Christo quasi deo dicere secum invicem seque sacramento non in scelus aliquod obstringere, sed ne furta ne latrocinia ne adulteria committerent, ne fidem fallerent, ne depositum adpellati abnegarent. … Conquirendi non sunt; si deferantur et arguantur, puniendi sunt, ita tamen ut, qui negaverit se Christianum esse idque re ipsa manifestum fecerit, id est supplicando dis nostris, quamvis suspectus in praeteritum, veniam ex paenitentia impetret.
excerpt_note: Two passages joined: the first sentence of Pliny's 10.96.7, then (after the ellipsis, which is Vocābula's, not the edition's) the first sentence of Trajan's reply, 10.97.2, from the separate DCC page https://dcc.dickinson.edu/pliny-letters/10-97. The DCC text prints macrons; they are removed here for tracing. The Perseus text of the letters (edition unnamed) spells Affirmabant and appellati.

translation: They declared, however, that the sum of their guilt, or their error, had been this: they used to meet on a fixed day before daybreak and chant a hymn among themselves, taking turns, to Christ as to a god, and to bind themselves by an oath, not to commit some crime, but not to commit theft, banditry or adultery, not to break their word, and not to deny holding a deposit when asked to return it. … [Trajan:] They are not to be hunted down. If they are reported and proved guilty, they must be punished, but on this condition: anyone who denies being a Christian and makes this plain in action, that is, by praying to our gods, is to be pardoned for his repentance, however suspect he may have been in the past.
translation_note: Pliny's sentence is reported speech after Adfirmābant: infinitives (fuisse, convenīre, dīcere, obstringere) and subjunctives (essent, committerent). Sēcum invicem probably means the chant was sung responsively, but "among themselves in turn" is the literal sense. Trajan's gerundives (conquīrendī, pūniendī) express obligation. Negāverit and fēcerit can be read as future perfect indicatives or perfect subjunctives; English uses the present.

essay.t: Pliny governed Bithynia and Pontus, on the Black Sea coast of Asia Minor, as Trajan's legate with consular power; an inscription (CIL V 5262) records the title.

The province was normally governed by a proconsul; the Judaism and Rome project explains that it was made temporarily imperial so Trajan could choose the governor, after years of financial trouble and disorder caused by factions.
The date is uncertain: Livius gives 109–111, the Judaism and Rome project "probably" 110–112, adding that Pliny died about 113, not long after this correspondence.

In another letter of Book 10, Pliny asks to form a guild of 150 firemen at Nicomedia after a great fire; Trajan refuses, warning that any group formed in that province would soon become a political club, a hetaeria.
The same rule surfaces here: the Christians said they had stopped their common meal after Pliny's edict, issued on Trajan's instructions, banned hetaeriae.
My reading: facing a new problem, the governor applied an existing rule and asked the centre, which declined to make a general law.
Pliny admits he had never attended a trial of Christians and did not know whether the name itself was punishable or only crimes attached to it.

He asked the accused up to three times, executed those who persisted, sent Roman citizens to Rome, and released those who invoked the gods, offered incense and wine to Trajan's image and cursed Christ.
Trajan approved: Christians were not to be sought out, but if accused and convicted they were punished, unless they recanted by praying to the gods; anonymous accusations were not to be accepted.
Scholars still disagree about the legal basis for punishing Christians at all.
Tertullian later summed the ruling up as: not to be sought out, but punished if brought forward; Davies judges his account accurate in substance.
For early Christian practice this is rare outside testimony, but it comes from people under interrogation, some of them former members, and may be shaped by what they hoped would save them.
Torturing two slave women called ministrae, "deaconesses", Pliny found nothing but "a depraved and excessive superstition".

questions.q: What did Trajan rule about Christians?
options: They were not to be hunted down, but punished if accused and convicted
They were to be hunted down everywhere
They were to be released in all cases
They were to be sent to Rome for trial

questions.q: Which earlier exchange between Pliny and Trajan shows the same worry about associations?
options: Trajan refused a guild of firemen at Nicomedia
Trajan refused to build an aqueduct

questions.q: How did people accused of being Christians prove they were not, according to Pliny and Trajan?
options: By praying to the gods, and for Pliny also offering to Trajan's image and cursing Christ
